Newly emerged rabbit fish (Chimaera monstrosa) neonates measure approximately 16.4 centimeters [Lb = approximately 16.4 centimeters] in total length at birth, a value derived from morphometric relationships between precaudal length and overall body size. This modest size at parturition reflects the relatively small yolk-dependent embryos that develop within the protective egg capsule during the prolonged incubation period characteristic of chimaeroid fishes. Following the absorption of the internal yolk sac and the onset of independent foraging, these young individuals embark on a slow but steady growth trajectory. The species is known to attain a considerable ultimate total length, with large, reproductively senescent adults reported to reach up to 150 centimeters [Li = up to 150 centimeters] in total length, making Chimaera monstrosa one of the larger members of the family Chimaeridae in the North Atlantic. This substantial final size, coupled with a later age at maturation, suggests a life-history strategy skewed toward elevated adult survivorship rather than high fecundity, a pattern common among deep-water chondrichthyans subject to low natural mortality rates in their cold, stable benthic environment.

Size at which puberty is attained in rabbit fish shows notable variability between populations and sampling locations. In one well-studied aggregation from the northeastern Atlantic, the total length at puberty for females was estimated at 62.9 centimeters [Lp = 62.9 centimeters], based on a regression from precaudal length measurements and the observation of vitellogenic follicles. However, a separate analysis of individuals from a deeper slope region off the coast of Norway reported a comparatively smaller length at puberty of 55.7 centimeters [Lp = 55.7 centimeters], derived from the same precaudal scaling relationship. This disparity, amounting to over seven centimeters, may reflect differences in local productivity regimes or density-dependent growth patterns, as individuals from more food-limited environments often channel energy into somatic maintenance rather than early reproductive development. The onset of gonadal maturation in this species is a gradual process, with testicular recrudescence in males and ovarian follicle development in females spanning several years before the first successful copulation and subsequent fertilisation can occur.

Reproductive output in Chimaera monstrosa is constrained by the cold temperatures that dominate its deep-sea habitat. Under thermal conditions of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], the maximum reproductive rate for this species corresponds to approximately six offspring per year [Ri = approximately six offspring per year], representing the highest fecundity recorded in captivity for this species. Females typically deposit paired, leathery egg capsules onto the soft sediment of the continental slope, with each capsule containing a single fertilised ovum. The observed annual production of egg cases, combined with the extended incubation period necessary for embryonic development at these low temperatures, limits the frequency of reproductive events. Females produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and, under optimal conditions, may deposit up to three clutches each year [F_R_i = up to three clutches each year], yielding a maximum of approximately six offspring annually. This slow reproductive turnover makes the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as population recovery from even modest fishing pressure can require multiple decades.

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown, senescent individuals of Chimaera monstrosa is considerable, with the largest specimens on record reaching up to 2.5 kilograms [Wwi = up to 2.5 kilograms]. This substantial body mass is supported by a cartilaginous skeleton and a lipid-rich liver that contributes significantly to buoyancy control in the species' deep-water environment. The slow, deliberate growth to this maximum size is reflected in the extended lifespan reported for this species. When maintained under stable thermal conditions of 6 °C, a temperature regime typical of the depths they inhabit, the maximum lifespan recorded for Chimaera monstrosa is approximately thirty years [am = approximately thirty years] at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. This longevity places the rabbit fish among the longer-lived chondrichthyans, exceeding the lifespan estimates for many coastal sharks and rays and underscoring the extreme K-selected life-history strategy that governs its population dynamics. Tags recaptured after extended periods have confirmed individual ages exceeding thirty years in some wild populations.

In comparative terms, the life-history parameters of Chimaera monstrosa align closely with those of other bathyal chondrichthyans, including the related elephant fish (Callorhinchus milii), though the rabbit fish attains a greater ultimate length at maturity. The extended period of juvenile growth, lasting many years before the first pupping event, imposes a demographic lag that makes the species exceptionally sensitive to increased adult mortality from deep-water trawling. Population viability models parameterized with these empirical growth and reproductive values consistently predict slow recovery rates even under moderate harvest scenarios. The stable temperatures at depth, which rarely deviate from 6 °C, are a key environmental driver shaping the low metabolic rates and protracted developmental timelines observed across all life stages. Understanding these physiological constraints is critical for the development of effective, age-structured management plans that can ensure the long-term persistence of this enigmatic and ecologically important holocephalan in the face of expanding deep-sea fisheries.
